executive_summary: The most important connecting thread across today's content is the accelerating crisis of institutional credibility — in technology, law enforcement, and the legal system simultaneously. The Musk v. Altman trial, as detailed in MIT Technology Review, has collapsed into a binary credibility contest between two men whose competing portraits each reveal a tech leadership class that is either self-dealing or power-obsessed, undermining public trust in the AI institutions shaping civilization's near-term future. That same erosion of institutional trust is visible in the breaking news cycle: an ICE agent charged with shooting a Venezuelan immigrant and a fatal mosque shooting in San Diego each, in different ways, raise urgent questions about the legitimacy and accountability of authority. The Economist's examination of data centre backlash adds a third dimension — public skepticism toward the physical infrastructure of the very AI industry whose leaders are now on trial. Taken together, these stories do not merely coexist; they reflect a single systemic tension in which the institutions Americans rely on — law enforcement, the courts, and the technology sector — are simultaneously under pressure to prove they deserve the power they hold.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions, although they still generally insist that the extra energy use is just a temporary measure to compensate for a lack of capacity on the electricity grid. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The final week of the Musk v. Altman trial reduced to a credibility contest between two rival portraits: Altman as a self-dealing liar and Musk as a power-hungry AGI control-seeker, with the jury now holding the decisive verdict.
longform.context: MIT Technology Review's courtroom correspondent Michelle Kim, who is also a lawyer, covered all three weeks of the Musk v. Altman trial in person; this newsletter dispatch summarizes the explosive final week as both legal teams made their closing attacks on the opposing principal's character and motives.
arguments: Musk's legal team attacked Altman's credibility by framing him as a liar engaged in self-dealing, targeting OpenAI's contested nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion as evidence of personal enrichment over mission integrity.

Altman's legal team countered by portraying Musk as a power-seeker whose lawsuit is motivated by a desire to control artificial general intelligence rather than protect OpenAI's founding mission, undermining the sincerity of his claimed idealism.

The trial surfaced new documentary and testimonial details about OpenAI's internal culture and governance disputes, including a 'golden trophy of a donkey's ass' awarded to an employee who challenged Musk — evidence used to illustrate Musk's retaliatory posture toward dissent within the organization.
longform.significance: The verdict will establish a legal and reputational precedent for how AI nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions are governed and contested, directly affecting OpenAI's restructuring plans and the broader AI industry's governance norms. The trial also airs, under oath and with documentary evidence, the founding mythology of the most consequential AI lab in the world — mythology that has shaped public and regulatory understanding of OpenAI's mission. The parallel reporting on Trump trading tech stocks before issuing favorable policy decisions for those same companies compounds the piece's relevance to questions of who actually controls AI's trajectory.
questions_raised: Whether the jury's verdict on credibility will translate into a legally actionable finding on OpenAI's nonprofit obligations — or whether the case ultimately turns on contract and fiduciary law rather than the character contest played out in closing arguments.

If Musk is found to have sought AGI control for competitive rather than altruistic reasons, what legal or regulatory mechanism exists to prevent any single actor — including Altman — from exercising equivalent control over a restructured, for-profit OpenAI?

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters I/O 2026 as a clear third-place foundation model competitor, facing a credible coding deficit against Anthropic and OpenAI while retaining a meaningful but underappreciated lead in AI for science.
longform.context: MIT Technology Review's Grace Huckins previews Google's annual developer conference I/O 2026, writing on the eve of the event amid a competitive landscape that has shifted sharply against Google since I/O 2025, when Gemini 2.5 Pro briefly placed the company near the frontier.
arguments: Google's coding tools have fallen so far behind Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex that DeepMind engineers were reportedly permitted to use Claude for internal work — a concrete, embarrassing signal of competitive failure that a single I/O announcement is unlikely to reverse, even with a new DeepMind coding team and Nobel laureate John Jumper lending his expertise.

Science and health remain Google's 'conspicuous strength': the company holds the only Nobel Prize among frontier AI labs, released tools like AI co-scientist (described as an 'oracle' by a Stanford scientist) and AlphaEvolve in the past year, and leads in LLM-based health research — though OpenAI has seized the health AI narrative since ChatGPT Health's January launch, and Google's forthcoming Health Coach appears narrowly scoped to fitness and diet rather than clinical concerns.

Google faces internal and reputational pressure that Hassabis's 'Nobel Prize-winning nerd' persona obscures: 600 employees, many from DeepMind, protested a pending DoD contract in an open letter to Sundar Pichai, and Google signed the deal the following day — a controversy that will shadow the conference even as executives work to project neutrality.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it reframes the AI competition narrative away from a two-horse race between OpenAI and Anthropic, positioning Google not as a co-leader but as a company in active retreat on the metric — coding — that currently defines frontier model reputation. It also draws attention to Google's science and health portfolio as a substantively distinct competitive dimension that industry coverage routinely underweights, suggesting that the standard leaderboard framing misses where Google's long-term leverage may actually lie.
questions_raised: Whether Google's restraint in deploying health AI tools reflects 'appropriate caution in a high-stakes domain' or a strategic failure to define the category — a question Huckins raises directly but leaves unresolved.

How sustainable Hassabis's posture of 'neutrality' is given the DoD deal controversy and the broader politicization of AI procurement, particularly as competitor CEOs become increasingly vocal and Google's internal dissent becomes public.
